body.hook: Your band instrument might be the most expensive thing you've ever been responsible for. Brass and woodwind instruments are precise machines: a bent rod, a dented slide or a dropped mouthpiece can stop an instrument from playing. Learning to assemble, hold and care for it properly is the first skill every musician learns.

study.title: Instrument Care Station
study.question: How do I set up and care for my instrument?
study.passage:
Part 1, Assembly demonstration (10 minutes): Sit in sections. The teacher demonstrates assembly for each instrument family:
• Flute: twist the headjoint and footjoint gently; never push on the keys or rods.
• Clarinet and saxophone: grease corks lightly; moisten the reed; line up the reed with the mouthpiece tip and tighten the ligature gently. Hold the clarinet's middle joints without squeezing the rings and keys.
• Trumpet, trombone, French horn, euphonium and tuba: insert the mouthpiece with a gentle twist, never by banging it. Check the slides and valves move freely.
• Percussion: check sticks and mallets, and stand at the correct height for the snare and bells.
Part 2, Posture check (5 minutes): Sit tall at the front of the chair, feet flat, shoulders relaxed, instrument brought to you (not you to it).
Part 3, Breathing (5 minutes): Breathe in for 4 counts through the mouth, filling low in the body, then breathe out for 8 counts on a "ssss" sound.
Part 4, First sound (10 minutes): Mouthpiece only for brass (buzz), mouthpiece and barrel or neck for woodwinds, headjoint only for flute. Make a steady sound for 4 counts.
Part 5, Care and storage (5 minutes): Swab or dry the instrument, remove and store reeds in a reed case, close the case latches, and store the case flat.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.hook: Every great band sound starts with air. Professional players say "the air is the engine": without steady, supported breath, even the best instrument sounds thin and wobbly.

study.title: The Air Is the Engine
study.question: How does breathing shape my sound?
study.passage:
Breathing routine (written for this lesson; percussion students do the breathing and then practise steady stroke-by-stroke sound on a practice pad):
1. Posture check: sit tall on the front edge of the chair, feet flat, shoulders relaxed.
2. Belly breath: hand on stomach; breathe in through the mouth for 4 counts. Your hand should move out, not your shoulders up.
3. Breathe in 4, out 4 on a "too" sound; in 4, out 8; in 4, out 12; in 4, out 16. Keep the air speed even to the end.
4. Paper test: hold a sheet of paper against a wall with only air; keep it there for 8 counts.
5. Mouthpiece buzz or headjoint: brass buzz on the mouthpiece; flute on the headjoint; reeds on mouthpiece and barrel or neck. Hold 8 counts steady.
6. Long tones on the instrument: Concert F for 8 counts at 60 BPM. Listen: does the sound stay the same from start to end?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.hook: Your first notes are a big moment. Most bands start on the same five concert pitches so everyone can play together from day one: Concert B♭, C, D, E♭ and F.

study.title: First Five Notes
study.question: How do I play my first notes with good tone?
study.passage:
First notes (written for this lesson): The band plays Concert B♭ C D E♭ F. Because some instruments transpose, the written note differs:
Flute, oboe, bassoon, trombone, baritone, tuba, mallet percussion: read B♭ C D E♭ F.
B♭ clarinet, B♭ trumpet, tenor saxophone: read C D E F G.
Alto and baritone saxophone (E♭ instruments): read G A B C D.
French horn (F): read F G A B♭ C.
Snare and percussion: play the rhythm on a pad with even strokes.
Steps: 1. Find each note on your fingering chart. 2. Tongue "too" to start each note; keep air flowing between notes. 3. Play each note for 4 counts at 72 BPM, resting 4 counts. 4. Play up and down the five notes. 5. Tone check: is the sound full and clear, not thin or buzzy? Adjust embouchure and air.
Partner check: one plays, one listens for clean starts and steady tone.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; transpositions follow standard band practice.
